title: The five SOLID principles
idea: SOLID is five design rules for classes; each one guards against a specific way code becomes hard to change, test or extend.
points: Single Responsibility (SRP) and Open/Closed (OCP) decide where code lives and how behaviour arrives.
Liskov Substitution (LSP) and Interface Segregation (ISP) keep contracts honest and interfaces small.
Dependency Inversion (DIP) makes policy depend on interfaces, so details plug in from outside.
They are smell detectors, not laws; apply one when its pain actually appears.

steps.caption: A request arrives: welcome new users by SMS. SRP asks which actor (team asking for changes) wants it; only welcome code should change.
OCP asks whether SMS can arrive as a new `SmsWelcome` class, leaving `Registration` and its tests untouched.
LSP asks whether `SmsWelcome` keeps the `Welcome` promise: return text, never null or a surprise exception.
ISP asks whether registration sees only what it needs. `UserWriter` has one method, so a list can stand in.
DIP asks who creates the parts. The caller injects policy, writer and welcomes, so a test can pass fakes.
Five questions, one result: one new class and one wiring line. No tested class was reopened.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A small sign-up service with one smell per letter, each marked in a comment.

walk.text: S: the password rule, storage and welcome text change for different teams, yet share one class.
O: each welcome channel is a `switch` branch, so a new channel reopens tested code.
L: `ArchivedUsers` is a `UserStore` that throws on `save`. Callers cannot trust the parent type.
I: sign-up needs only `save`, but the interface also forces `delete` and `all`.
D: the service builds its own concrete store, so a test cannot swap in a fake.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Each smell gets its own small fix. SMS arrives as a new class, and a list stands in for storage.

walk.text: S: the password rule is its own type, so changing it never touches registration.
I: `UserWriter` asks for one method, so `saved::add` fits.
O + L: each channel is a class behind `Welcome`, and each keeps the promise to return text.
D: policy, writer and channels arrive through the constructor; the map is copied.
Unknown channels fail before the user is saved, so no half-registered user exists.
Main wires the parts. A list replaces the database, which is what DIP buys in tests.

pitfalls: An interface for every class with one implementation doubles your files and buys nothing.
Reciting the five letters in an interview without naming the change each protects sounds memorised.
Applying all five to a 50-line script slows you down; wait until a change hurts.

quiz.q: A `PaymentService` gains a new `if` branch for every payment method. Which principle does that break first?
quiz.why: Each new payment method edits tested code. OCP wants new methods to arrive as new classes behind one interface, leaving the service closed.

takeaway: SOLID names five pains of change; fix the one you feel.
